The exact firmware flash bytes that produced the result, independently of the match-behaviour hash.
Match behaviour has a separate hash; build identity concerns the programmed image.

topicTitle: The Host League — Thirty Files, One Program
question: Why sort entries after constructor registration?
options: Sorting adjusts each strategy's gains to equal values.
Constructors always run in alphabetical strategy order.
Sorting removes constructor/link-order variation from tournament order.
explanations: It orders entries for reproducibility; it does not alter strategy behaviour.
Object and link order can vary; explicit sorting gives stable order.
Constructor and object link order can vary; sorting stabilises tournament ordering and reproducibility.

topicTitle: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
question: Which check validates the submission scheme's cross-platform assumption?
options: Matching source names guarantees matching host/chip floating-point outcomes.
Compare seeded chip and host behaviour hashes alongside build/budget checks.
Compare host graphics screenshots only.
explanations: The same seeded run and behaviour hash directly check the cross-platform assumption.
Run the chip tournament with the same seed and compare its behaviour hash with the host's, alongside budget/build checks.
Screenshots do not check deterministic chip tournament behaviour or execution budgets.

question: Name four deliberate ingredients of repeatable matches.
options: A fixed seed alone, with arbitrary sensing order and persistent state.
Isolated state, independent seeded RNG, simultaneous sensing and consistent arithmetic.
Shared static state, one conditional RNG stream, sequential sensing and fused arithmetic.
explanations: A seed cannot compensate for shared state, unequal snapshots or differing arithmetic sequences.
Isolated per-robot state, independent seeded RNG streams, simultaneous sensing and consistent non-fused floating-point arithmetic.
Each introduces coupling or cross-platform/order dependence opposite to the intended repeatability rules.

question: Which pins carry OLED data and clock, and what else must its wiring include?
options: PB8 is SDA and PB9 is SCL; use address 0x68.
PB9 SDA, PB8 SCL, 3V3, common ground and OLED address 0x3C.
PB9 and PB8 suffice without a shared ground.
explanations: This swaps clock and data and uses the MPU6050 address rather than OLED address 0x3C.
PB9 is SDA and PB8 SCL; connect 3V3 and ground and use the configured I²C bus and device address 0x3C.
The display also needs power and a common ground; signal pins alone do not complete its electrical connection.

question: What does the knob control in this lesson?
options: The knob always commands throttle in every final project.
Application-defined inputs; PA5 blinks while watchdog refresh is allowed.
PA5 blinks only when the OLED finishes a frame.
explanations: The application defines its controls; the template forwards buttons, joystick and knob.
Buttons, joystick and knob feed the application; PA5 blinks while watchdog refresh is permitted.
Its template indication follows permitted watchdog refresh rather than display completion.

question: Which MODER bits select PB8 mode, and what values support I²C?
options: MODER bits 17:16 select analog mode 11 with AF6.
MODER bits 8:8 select output mode 01; AFR6 is sufficient.
MODER bits 17:16 = 10, AFR = AF6, with open-drain and pull-ups.
explanations: Analog mode disconnects the alternate digital peripheral; I²C needs alternate mode and open-drain/pull-up configuration.
MODER allocates two bits per pin, so PB8 occupies bits 17:16 and needs alternate mode 10.
Bits 17:16 hold pin 8 mode. Set 10 for alternate mode and the appropriate AFR field to AF6; I²C also needs its electrical/open-drain and pull-up setup.

question: Why is setting only AFR insufficient?
options: AFR selects routing; MODER must also activate alternate mode.
AFR automatically changes MODER to alternate mode.
AFR only controls clock frequency.
explanations: AFR selects the peripheral routing, but MODER must also enable alternate mode or the pin is not connected to that function.
These are separate fields; selecting a route does not activate that route.
AFR chooses which peripheral signal reaches a pin; it is not a peripheral clock divider.

topicTitle: What You Are About to Build
question: What must be demonstrable by week 4?
options: Every planned stretch feature, even before the MVP works.
A running end-to-end Wokwi MVP with host tests passing.
A complete report with no running integration.
explanations: The gate concerns the smallest working system, not optional stretch work.
An end-to-end MVP running in Wokwi with its host tests passing, rather than isolated unfinished components.
Week 4 requires the end-to-end MVP running in Wokwi and host checks passing.

topicTitle: What a Good Embedded Project Looks Like
question: Why can a small game outscore a half-complete 3 D maze?
options: Complexity alone earns full working-system marks.
A complete modest project can satisfy the actual evidence criteria.
A small game's timing and fault handling do not count toward grading.
explanations: The rubric awards demonstrated behaviour and engineering evidence, not feature count.
It can fully satisfy working behaviour, timing, fault, test and explanation criteria; complexity alone earns none of those assurances.
Those are explicit evidence criteria and can make a modest complete project score well.

question: What common interface principle links game and drone tracks?
options: Both must share identical OLED rendering code to be testable.
Both cores should read peripheral clocks internally to decide dt.
Portable core logic accepts explicit inputs/time and produces outputs/state.
explanations: The shared principle is a hardware-independent logic interface, not a particular display driver.
Explicit time and inputs separate portable logic from platform details.
Hardware-independent logic receives explicit inputs/time and produces outputs/state, enabling replay and host testing.

question: Which measures distinguish a polished game from a merely running one?
options: Average frame rate alone, regardless of worst input delay.
Only the screenshot's colour palette.
Frame rate, worst input delay, bus bytes and long-run correctness.
explanations: A good average can hide slow reactions or failures; the listed worst-case and robustness measures also matter.
Polish here includes measured responsiveness, frame/bus cost and robust long-run behaviour.
Frame rate, worst input latency, bus bytes per frame and long-run random-input correctness.

question: Why record fault detection and action times separately?
options: Detection time automatically equals actuator action time.
Only the time of the injected fault matters.
Detection can be prompt while the later safety action is delayed.
explanations: Scheduling and processing after detection can delay the actual response.
The interval to detection and the interval to action together establish response latency.
A quick detector can still be followed by a delayed response; both stages determine the actual safety latency.

question: Why state N and seeds with a robot win-rate claim?
options: Seeds are aesthetic labels with no impact on a trial.
N=1 establishes general win rate if that one match was won.
N and seeds state trial breadth and reproducible conditions.
explanations: They identify reproducible random conditions; N states how many trials support the rate.
A single favourable outcome provides too little coverage for a broad claim.
They define reproducibility and breadth of the trial; one favourable match does not establish general performance.

question: What three conditions apply to the original-project option, Track D?
options: Only instructor approval; execution platform and core structure are optional.
Base-board Wokwi, a host-tested pure-C core and agreed measurable scope.
Any hardware platform, no host checks, and unrestricted scope.
explanations: Agreement is one of three conditions rather than a replacement for the other two.
Base-board Wokwi execution, a pure-C core tested on host and instructor agreement to measurable proposal scope.
Track D still needs base-board Wokwi operation, a host-tested pure-C core and agreed measurable scope.

question: Is a working physics engine with no usable output an MVP?
options: Yes; an unused physics engine is equivalent to a demonstrated product.
No; the smallest full user experience must run end-to-end.
Yes; any independently running component is a complete MVP.
explanations: Internal mechanics alone do not let the user exercise the proposed experience.
No. The smallest full user experience must run end-to-end, even with limited content or rough presentation.
The MVP is the smallest end-to-end user experience, which needs usable output.

question: Input, app and display periods are 10, 20 and 50 ms. What is their scheduling-only worst input latency?
options: 30 ms, because display cannot add latency.
50 ms, because display period is the only delay.
80 ms before display transfer, from 10+20+50.
explanations: An app update can wait for the next 50 ms display release too.
Worst phase waits also include input 10 ms and app 20 ms, totaling 80 ms before transfer.
10+20+50=80 ms, then add display transfer; it fails a 70 ms maximum without design changes.

question: Why label each shared-data arrow with its protection?
options: It makes ownership and synchronization visible for review.
Protection labels automatically implement a mutex in compiled code.
Arrows need only variable names because ownership cannot affect races.
explanations: It exposes ownership and races during design review instead of leaving synchronisation implicit.
They document a design contract; code must implement the chosen protection.
Ownership and synchronization determine who may change data and when.

question: Why intentionally give 100 ms telemetry higher priority than 50 ms display?
options: Shorter period always requires higher priority with no exception.
Telemetry has higher priority because its I²C transfer is longer than the display's.
Timely short telemetry outranks a display that tolerates slight lateness.
explanations: This design accounts for tolerable screen lateness and timely short telemetry work.
Telemetry is short UART work; the long polled display flush should not delay it.
A screen tolerates small lateness, while short telemetry work benefits from regular timestamps and should not be delayed by long display flushes.

question: Why copy the latest button level but accumulate its press edge?
options: Levels show current state; pending edges preserve unconsumed events.
Replace pending edges with every newest sample.
Accumulate button levels forever after the first press.
explanations: Level describes current state; edge records an event that must remain pending until the slower consumer receives it.
A brief event can vanish between slower app runs; edges must remain pending until consumed.
Levels describe current state and must replace old levels; only events need accumulation.

question: Why should shell request profiler reset rather than zero counters itself?
options: Every task should reset every other task's counter for consistency.
The periodic task remains its counter's sole writer.
Shell writes zero safely because aligned stores prevent all races.
explanations: One writer per counter plus a reset request keeps ownership explicit.
Each periodic task remains the single writer, avoiding races with in-progress timing updates.
It can race with the owning task's update even if a single store is untorn.

question: Why must app_draw be read-only?
options: draw may mutate state on target but must be read-only on host.
Drawing should advance physics so faster displays improve gameplay.
Logic advances only in app_step, independently of rendering rate.
explanations: Different rules would break replay and cross-platform consistency.
That makes logic depend on refresh rate; state transitions belong to app_step.
Rendering rate and host/target differences must not advance game logic or change results; state changes belong to app_step.

question: The watchdog clock is nominally 32 kHz; PR=3 divides it by 32 and RLR=999 gives 1000 counts. Find the nominal timeout.
options: 32 s, because PR=3 multiplies the watchdog clock by 32.
Nominally 1 s, subject to the actual independent oscillator frequency.
999/32000≈31 ms, ignoring the divider.
explanations: The prescaler divides the clock, giving 1000 Hz and 1000 reload counts.
(999+1)/(32000/32)=1 s, subject to actual LSI frequency.
PR=3 selects divide-by-32 and RLR counts include +1, giving nominal 1 s.

question: Why use independent counters rather than a shared alive bitmap?
options: A shared bitmap OR is atomic across every preemption.
Single-writer counters avoid shared bitmap read-modify-write races.
Counters require a shared writer in health to increment every task's heartbeat.
explanations: Read-modify-write can overwrite another task's newly set bit.
Counters have one writer each. A preempted bitmap OR could overwrite another task's newer bit.
Each task owns its own counter; health observes progress rather than manufacturing it.

topicTitle: Failsafes — Defined Behaviour for Every Fault
question: Why can software recover hang display but not spin input?
options: A blocked display necessarily blocks the CPU forever.
A spinning top-priority task still allows health to run every 250 ms.
Blocked display lets health run; top-priority spinning input starves it.
explanations: A blocked task yields execution, allowing health to detect the missing heartbeat.
It starves all lower priorities, including the software fallback.
The blocked display allows health to run. A top-priority spinning input task prevents the fallback code from executing.

question: A full OLED frame sends 1088 bytes, each taking 22.5 µs. Calculate load when repeated at 20 Hz.
options: 100%, because any polled transfer permanently occupies the core.
4.9%, by dropping a factor of ten in frame rate.
About 49%: 1088×22.5 µs×20 per second.
explanations: Polling occupies CPU during transfer, not necessarily the entire second.
A 24.5 ms frame repeated 20 times uses 490 ms each second, or 49%.

question: Why can a simple telemetry task need hundreds of stack bytes?
options: UART hardware stores printf's call frames in peripheral memory.
Formatting and UART library calls add substantial call-chain stack.
Only the task's visible local variables use stack.
explanations: Call frames occupy the processor stack even when output eventually reaches a peripheral.
Its formatting and UART library chain consumes substantial stack before its own local variables.
Formatting and UART call chains add stack frames below that task.

question: Which statistic tests whether a task meets its deadline?
options: Maximum stack usage alone below 75%.
Peak response below the deadline, with no over-period runs.
Average CPU share alone below 100%.
explanations: Stack margin checks memory safety, not wake-to-completion deadline timing.
Maximum response compared with period, with over count zero; response includes higher-priority interference.
Low average utilization can coexist with missed individual deadlines; compare peak response and over count.

topicTitle: The Test Plan, Part 1 — Host Tests
question: Why evaluate an assertion condition once?
options: A side-effectful condition can change on the second evaluation.
Assertions must call state-changing logic once for printing and again for checking.
Evaluating twice always increases confidence even when the call changes state.
explanations: A state-changing call such as health_check can behave differently on the second evaluation and produce false failure.
Store the single evaluated result and use it for both checking and reporting.
A side effect can change the second result, giving a misleading assertion failure.

topicTitle: The Test Plan, Part 2 — What You Will Watch in Wokwi
question: What belongs in a target observation log?
options: Only an unlabelled screenshot with no triggering action.
Only the expected behaviour, since the demo should match it.
Action, expectation, observed evidence and relevant simulator limitations.
explanations: A reproducible log records action, expectation, observed result and relevant simulator limits.
Actual observations and evidence are needed to compare claims with results.
What was done, expected and seen, with screenshots/recordings/logs and any simulator limitation affecting the result.

question: What action is expected if MVP slips beyond week 4?
options: Report the missed gate and reduce scope.
Hide the delay until final demonstration.
Add more stretch features to compensate for the missing core.
explanations: Report it during review and cut scope; do not hide the missed gate.
The missed gate must be disclosed and scope reduced to remain deliverable.
That increases risk instead of restoring a feasible MVP.

question: What must accompany a reproducible live demo?
options: Tagged code, report, measured requirements, sustained stats and a fault demo.
A video from any older build without a code tag.
Only a slide claiming all requirements passed.
explanations: Tagged code, report PDF, measured requirement results, sustained-run stats and a demonstrated fault response.
The live result must trace to tagged code and current measured evidence.
The demo also needs the report, sustained statistics and a demonstrated fault response.

question: What caps apply to warnings and contradicted report claims?
options: Both categories are automatically zero for one warning.
Engineering remains capped at 15 and report at 10 regardless of evidence.
Warnings cap engineering at 8; contradicted claims cap report at 3.
explanations: The documented caps are 8 and 3 rather than universal zeros.
Warnings cap engineering at 8 and contradicted claims cap the report at 3.
Engineering quality is capped at 8; the report is capped at 3 when the demo contradicts a claim.

question: What information must AI disclosure include?
options: Only the model name; understanding generated code is optional.
Only code edits; AI use need not be identified if the program runs.
Tool, purpose and author changes, with understanding and verification.
explanations: Disclose tool, use and changes, and explain and independently verify the resulting code.
The policy requires tool and purpose disclosure as well as author changes and understanding.
The tool, its use and what authors changed; they must also explain and verify resulting code.

topicTitle: What Was Measured — and What Could Not Be
question: Does host health success verify the physical IWDG?
options: No; host logic does not execute the silicon watchdog reset.
Yes; the host executes the hardware watchdog oscillator.
Yes; matching register names proves that the silicon reset happened.
explanations: No. Register setup and silicon watchdog reset require separate evidence from host logic.
Host health tests check logic, not the silicon's independent oscillator or reset.
Register consistency is design evidence; actual reset behaviour needs separate execution evidence.

question: Which part is most portable to a new chip?
options: Pure-C logic with explicit inputs/time is most portable.
Only a Wokwi wiring diagram.
Peripheral register addresses and interrupt-vector names.
explanations: Pure-C logic with explicit time and inputs; peripheral drivers and scheduling bindings change.
The diagram binds hardware; the core algorithm can transfer through equivalent driver contracts.
Those depend on the chip and platform; explicit-input pure-C logic is the portable portion.

question: What happens when the mixer correction sign is reversed?
options: It only reverses the OLED's roll label.
It reduces effective gain but preserves stabilizing feedback.
It reinforces the tilt, creating positive feedback.
explanations: The mixer changes applied torque, so a reversed sign reinforces physical tilt.
A sign reversal turns negative feedback into positive feedback rather than merely weakening it.
A correction intended to oppose tilt increases it instead, making positive feedback. Verify coordinate and motor sign conventions before increasing gains.

question: Why does a saturated actuator need anti-windup?
options: Integral should keep growing to force the actuator beyond its limit.
It prevents an impossible accumulated request from causing later overshoot.
Saturation automatically clears accumulated integral error.
explanations: The actuator cannot exceed its range, and stored impossible correction causes overshoot later.
The integral can keep growing while the requested command is impossible, causing prolonged overshoot after the error changes. Bound or condition integration according to the controller design.
A clipped command does not erase the accumulator; integration must be bounded or conditional.

question: What can the browser’s one-axis model establish?
options: It measures real IMU bus latency.
It proves a physical three-axis drone safe.
It illustrates estimator and feedback mechanisms within a limited one-axis model.
explanations: The one-axis software model illustrates mechanisms, not the physical bus.
The browser omits three-axis dynamics, interfaces and execution timing.

It illustrates estimator and feedback mechanisms. It omits full three-axis dynamics, task timing, and sensor interfaces. A stable browser trace alone does not prove that a physical drone is safe or stable.

question: Why does a delayed GPS reading need more than a present-time correction?
options: A delayed reading describes the state at its arrival time.
It describes an earlier state; the estimator must account for observation age.
A checksum removes measurement age.
explanations: It describes an earlier measurement time, so treating it as current adds lag and inconsistency.
It describes an earlier state. Applying it as if current can inject lag and inconsistency. The estimator must handle observation age according to its design.
Transmission integrity does not make an old observation current.

question: How should conflicting low-battery and mission commands resolve?
options: The newest command always wins, including a mission request.
Documented safety priorities make critical-battery protection outrank mission commands.
A mission must finish before any battery action.
explanations: Safety priorities must prevent a mission command overriding critical-battery protection.
The documented safety priority decides the mode. A mission request must not override critical-battery landing or other higher-priority protection.
That can exhaust the battery; critical safety conditions take precedence.

question: What must be validated before executing uploaded waypoints?
options: Validate protocol structure, ranges, coordinates, storage bounds and timeouts.
Coordinates need validation only after the aircraft starts following them.
A checksum alone proves every waypoint safe and well formed.
explanations: Count, lengths, sequence/order, ranges, coordinates and checksums as specified by the protocol, plus bounded storage and timeout behavior. Receiving bytes is not permission to fly them.
Reject malformed or unsafe mission data before execution.
Counts, sequence, ranges, coordinates and bounded storage also require validation.

question: Why is “line lost” not error zero?
options: Lost means insufficient position evidence; centered means a valid zero error.
The previous numerical zero can always be reused forever.
The sensor weight is low, so the robot is certainly centered.
explanations: Zero is positive evidence of being centered. Lost means the sensor weight is too low to estimate position; a recovery/search rule must handle that state.
Loss requires a bounded recovery/search rule instead of assuming a current measurement.
Low weight means insufficient evidence, while centered is a valid position estimate.

question: Why can increasing Kd worsen a noisy run?
options: Kd affects only steady-state error, so sample timing is irrelevant.
A larger derivative gain suppresses every sensor fluctuation.
Derivative action amplifies fast changes, including noise, and depends on dt.
explanations: Derivative depends on error changes over dt; filtering and timing affect it.
Derivative action amplifies rapid changes and can amplify noise.
A derivative amplifies rapid sample changes. Filtering and dt affect the computed derivative; tune using the same sampling conditions and inspect noise.

question: Why do encoder counts not guarantee ground distance?
options: Both wheels turning equally guarantees accurate ground distance.
Encoders directly measure the robot's world coordinates.
Encoders measure wheel rotation; slip can separate it from ground travel.
explanations: Both can slip equally; wheel rotation alone does not prove translation.
They measure wheel rotation, which must be converted through a physical model.
Encoders measure wheel rotation. Slip means the wheel can rotate without matching translation across the ground. The plant and judging model distinguish those quantities.

question: Why inflate obstacles in a costmap?
options: Inflation corrects every localization bias automatically.
Inflation makes the robot's real body smaller.
It accounts for the robot's finite body and required obstacle clearance.
explanations: It models required clearance rather than fixing the pose estimate.
It adds map clearance to account for finite body size.
A point route near a wall can collide with the robot’s finite body. Inflation encodes required clearance around occupied cells.

question: Why can reactive braking stop motion even when a path exists?
options: An existing path proves every immediate beam reading safe.
Fresh local danger can override a path based on stale or incomplete belief.
Braking is useful only after global replanning completes.
explanations: The path can rely on stale or incomplete map belief.
The path may rely on stale or incomplete belief. A local observation can indicate immediate danger before global replanning finishes.
Immediate collision evidence must stop motion before slower planning catches up.

question: What does unknown assumed free trade off?
options: It enables exploration but risks unseen obstacles, requiring protective sensing/control.
Unknown-as-free removes the need for sensing and braking.
Unknown cells are physically guaranteed empty.
explanations: It enables exploration but risks planning through unseen obstacles. Sensing, safe speed, braking and replanning must compensate; unknown is not proven free.
Those safeguards are needed precisely because unseen obstacles may be present.
Unknown means unobserved, so free assumptions permit exploration at risk.

question: What does u=−Kx mean?
options: The minus sign is valid regardless of coordinate and plant conventions.
A plant-consistent weighted combination of full state errors commands the actuator.
u uses angle alone and ignores translation.
explanations: The sign and desired-state offsets must match the modeled plant.

The command is a weighted combination of state errors with a sign convention tied to the plant. x normally includes position, velocity, angle and angular rate; desired-state offsets must be accounted for.
Full state feedback normally combines position, velocity, angle and angular rate.

question: Does a stable linearized model prove recovery from any lean?
options: Yes; eigenvalues automatically enforce the robot's mechanical constraints.
Yes; a stable local model covers all angles and motor limits.
No; local linear stability does not cover arbitrary lean or saturation.
explanations: Mathematical local stability does not impose physical travel or voltage limits.
Linearization is local, and nonlinearities or saturation can prevent recovery.
No. Linearization applies near its operating point. Large angles, saturation and physical constraints can put the nonlinear system outside the stabilizable region.

question: Why compare controller variants under the same disturbance?
options: Use different payloads so every controller sees its best case.
Common repeatable conditions isolate the control-law change.
A larger push on the preferred controller makes the comparison controlled.
explanations: That confounds controller effects with a changed plant.
Changing payload, initial state, sensors or disturbance changes the experiment. A repeatable common input makes the control-law comparison interpretable.
Changing disturbances changes the experiment; use common repeatable input.

question: Why is using world coordinates in a strategy unfair?
options: Truth is merely another allowed sensor reading.
Only the viewer's graphics determine whether a strategy is fair.
True positions bypass the strategy's restricted sensor contract.
explanations: The strategy contract limits knowledge to observations, excluding simulator truth.
The strategy's information access determines fairness even if graphics are unchanged.
The contract restricts knowledge to sensor observations. True positions bypass sensing uncertainty and opponent visibility, invalidating the comparison.

question: Why do both robots sense before either is advanced?
options: Sequential movement is fair because both calls take the same CPU time.
Sensing first removes every random noise difference.
Both strategies decide from the same pre-movement world snapshot.
explanations: The second strategy still sees a later world snapshot.
It synchronizes observation time, not individual sensor noise.
It gives both decisions the same world snapshot. Sequential sense-and-move can make outcomes depend on loop order.

question: What evidence distinguishes a better strategy from a lucky round?
options: One win against one fixed starting pose.
Change physics and scoring for each strategy to maximize its score.
Repeated seeded trials with varied starts and fixed scoring/physics/timing.
explanations: A lucky round cannot support a broad strategy claim.
Comparable trials keep physics, timing and scoring fixed.
Repeated seeded trials, varied starting conditions and specified scoring. Keep physics, opponents and timing limits fixed while comparing the strategy change.

question: What makes “stops safely” a testable requirement?
options: Specify the fault, response bound, measurement method and trial conditions.
Only the intended safe state matters; response time cannot affect safety.
The phrase “stops safely” is measurable without any specified bound.
explanations: Specify the fault/input condition, maximum response time or stopping distance, measurement method and trial conditions. For example, a stale sensor sequence must cause zero wheel command within a stated time.
A delayed stop can be dangerous despite eventually reaching the safe state.
A test needs triggering conditions, response/distance limits and a measurement method.

question: Why should one owner write each actuator?
options: Every task should directly reset actuators whenever it finishes.
Multiple independent writers always react faster without conflicts.
One owner resolves explicit requests and priorities without conflicting output writes.
explanations: One owner with explicit priority handling preserves coordinated output decisions.
They can overwrite each other's safety and control commands.
Concurrent writers can overwrite safety and control decisions. Define one output owner and explicit requests/priorities so recovery cannot be undone by another task.

question: What should a submission demonstrate beyond a normal run?
options: A normal-run video alone proves timing and fault recovery.
Measured timing/memory, target behaviour, repeatable checks and fault recovery.
Host success establishes every electrical and target timing claim.
explanations: Measured timing, memory and injected-fault behaviour need separate evidence.

Show measured timing and memory, repeatable checks, behavior on the target board, and what happens when a fault is introduced. Define how the system recovers or reaches a safe state, and check required assignment deliverables in the optional references.
Target board behaviour requires target evidence, alongside repeatable host checks.
